3718.prule: Stress is lexically distributed within a right-edge three-syllable window, as in Castilian/Galician-Portuguese: words are oxytone (agudas: última sílaba tónica), paroxytone (llanas: penúltima), proparoxytone (esdrújulas: antepenúltima) or, with enclitic pronouns, pre-proparoxytone (sobreesdrújulas: cómpramulu); the position is marked per word by the tilde on Castilian-type conventions and is not derivable from syllable count or weight. Sub-regularity: words ending in a falling diphthong (au, ou, eu, ai, oi, ei) are final-stressed (falau, falei, pareceu, ademais, despois). Tonic/atonic monosyllable pairs contrast (dá/da, é/e, máis/mais, tó/to, sé/se).
3718.srule: Not mentioned in Valeš 2021 (front matter 'Ortografía' > 'Acentuación', pp. 28-29) or in ACANF 2017 ('Acintuación', pp. 7-8): both describe only the position of the single sílaba tónica (aguda / llana / isdrújula / sobriisdrújula) and tilde use; no secondary or rhythmic stress is mentioned there or in the other held works re-checked (Masa & Elordieta 2017, Elordieta & Masa 2020, Costas González 2021, Sánchez Domínguez 2022).

3721.prule: No word-stress rule is stated. Fáŋ is described as a tone language (underlying L, M, H per abstract/conclusion; ch. IV-1 lists L, M, H, S as 'the only underlying tones'; contours LH, HL, MH, HM are surface sequences). Stress is mentioned only generically ('unlike the stress, the tone is carried by a tone bearing unit'). Long vowels occur only in penultimate position and are shortened word-finally; the author quotes Mutaka & Tamanji's Bantu generalization that penultimate allophonic length is a manifestation of stress but does not apply it to Fáŋ, treating the long vowels as marginal phonemes/compensatory lengthening before prenasalized consonants.
3721.quote: [p.83] Fáŋ happens to be a tone language like most African languages. The tone is a prosodic unit which has the same value as the phonemic consonants and vowels. [...] Moreover, unlike the stress, the tone is carried by a tone bearing unit (TBU), which can be any segment that can function as the peak of the syllable. Now, one should notice that only vowels are tone bearing units in Fáŋ for there is no syllabic nasals or syllabic laterals in the language in hand. [...] [pp.40-41] During our analysis, we have come to realized that the existing long vowels in this language appear solely in penul…

3721.idn: Fáŋ (Féŋә́), the one-village language of Fang village, Lower Fungom, Wum subdivision, Menchum, North-West Region, Cameroon; explicitly distinguished from Beti-cluster Fang; data: Words and expressions collected through interviews with native speakers of Fáŋ resident in Fang village, Wum and Yaoundé…
3721.tone: Thesis ch. IV-V: Fáŋ is a tone language; abstract (p.iv) and conclusion give three underlying tones H, L, M, while IV-1 (p.83) says 'four attested level tones... L, M, H, S... the only underlying tones' with four surface contours (LH, HL, MH, HM) analysed as level-tone sequences; only vowels are TBUs. Stress/accent: the only 'stress' tokens are the generic p.83 contrast (tone is carried by a TBU 'unlike the stress') and the quoted Mutaka & Tamanji (2000:38) line on penultimate length as stress in Swahili/Chichewa/Kinande, which the author does not adopt for Fáŋ; no statement that Fáŋ has or lacks word stress. Good et al. 2011:148-149 (sec. 3.6.2) likewise give only consonants, vowels (root-initial vowel of tə̄wésə́ 'culverts' noticeably longer; length 'may be contrastive') and 'at least three tone levels' plus contours, with no stress/accent wording.

3726.dq: El acento prosódico cae en la penúltima sílaba de la palabra. [...] En la oración, las conjunciones y los verbos auxiliares no llevan acento. [...] La última palabra de la oración conserva el acento primario en la penúltima sílaba. [...] (Nimeque, a'ngomo, azúfre, pronunciadas solas, llevan el acento en la penúltima;)
3726.prule: Primary (prosodic) stress on the penultimate syllable of the whole inflected word, whatever morpheme that syllable belongs to (root, derivational or inflectional suffix, or enclitic): séma, copújtu, copùjtú'am, ø̀ngo'ndamutiná'ntzi. Weight plays no role; the rule is stated purely by position.
3726.srule: In words of four or more syllables a secondary stress falls on the first root, generally the first or second syllable of the word; it never falls on an affix, prefix or suffix (sèmapǿte, copùjtú'am, ø̀ngo'ndamutiná'ntzi). Two- and three-syllable words carry only the penultimate primary stress.

Sec. 6.4 establishes a word-level stress accent ('under the main accent', 'accented'/'unaccented' vowels, 'accented a') and, under her defined convention (p. vii, ˈ = tonic stress, ˌ = secondary stress), every Ganai item in sec. 6.4 and the Gippsland vocabulary (c. 120 items, pp. 240-242, all three pages checked item by item) carries ˈ on the first syllable, for 2-, 3-, 4- and 5-syllable words ([ˈbUndI], [ˈbandjəˌwɔn], [ˈbUlenˌdjetI], [ˈyindUˌbarkarʌ]); no simplex item shows non-initial primary stress. Hercus marks non-initial main accent where she hears it (Madimadi p. 116: consonants beginning the second syllable 'attracted the main accent into the second syllable'), so uniform initial marking is observation, not a default. Weight plays no role: long vowels are 'rare', conditioned, and partly a product of accent ('accented a before final d̪, dj and ṇ').

3740.prule: No stress rule is stated for Gane. The source states a transcription convention for all its wordlists: an unmarked word has penultimate stress; an acute marks any other stressed syllable. In the Gane column (109 items: Swadesh 100 shortened and nine words added, p. 129) 16 forms carry the acute: imlíf 'laugh', awós 'wash', ólai, maón, mapín, gagí, hawé, batól, gigyát, uát, lóal 'big', gamós, baloám, mikoát (note 13: Gane Luar), yagimsó, hafisák. Fourteen are final-stressed disyllables or trisyllables; two (ólai, lóal) carry the acute on the first vowel of a vowel sequence and may mark the syllabic peak rather than a third pattern. The other ~93 forms are unmarked, i.e. penultimate by convention; the unmarked Gane forms are positive readings, not missing data, because the same rows mark neighbouring languages differently (Gane kikle, tinge, mto, koku beside Wosi/Saketa/Kayoa kiklé, tingé, mtó, kokó). Final stress is not predictable from the transcription: unmarked closed-final words (wosal, katobat, manifis, abalit, makufin, milolang, langit, pwonam, lekat) sit beside marked batól, hafisák, gamós, mapín, and the marked forms show no schwa or other segmental trigger. The data therefore give a penultimate default with a lexically specified minority (about 15% of basic vocabulary) of final-stressed words: lexical stress with a penultimate default, derived from the data, not stated by the author.

3744.prule: Somali-type tonal accent: word accent is assigned to one MORA (not syllable) and realized as a single high tone; one H per word (culminative). Placement is not fixed by position or weight: most nouns (m. and f.) have H on the final mora, but many disyllabic nouns have H on the first mora; short-vowel monosyllables are H if masculine, L if feminine; long-vowel monosyllables have H on the first mora (falling). Verb H placement is set by tense/mood/person.
3744.srule: None: 'Ogni parola può avere un solo tono alto' — each word can have only one high tone, and the accented mora is that H (accent = tone); no secondary or rhythmic prominence is described (Tosco 1989 §1.4, pp. 23-25 read in full).

3744.tone: The source treats accent and tone as one thing ('accento e tono in K. coincidono'): the accented mora carries the word's single high tone, as in other Somali dialects and specifically as Saeed (1982: 8ff.) describes for Maay, rather than the tonology of Standard/Northern Somali (S.CS). No stress rule independent of tone is given; H placement is lexically variable in nouns (final mora for most, first mora for many disyllables, gender-conditioned in short-vowel monosyllables) and morphologically determined in verbs. The author flags the whole section as preliminary ('del tutto iniziale'), says nothing can be said yet about tonal case marking or main-vs-dependent verb tone, and notes verb tone patterns seem sensitive to sentence intonation and perhaps clause type.

tn.translation: As in the other Somali dialects, accent and tone coincide in K., in the sense that the mora — and not the syllable — to which word accent is assigned is realized with a high tone (´). Each word can have only one high tone. As in Maay, most nouns — masculine as well as feminine — have a high tone on the last mora: (24) ukúr (m.) 'navel' ... Many disyllables, masculine and feminine, instead have a high tone on the first mora: (25) bábbas (m.) 'ash' ... Monosyllables with a short vowel have high tone if masculine, low if feminine

3745.dq: A) The words are basically stressed on the last syllable. Any deviation from this rule is shown by an acute accent over the syllable to be stressed, and it is only in the case of such exceptions that the accent is used to indicate stress.
3745.dloc: p. 734, sec. IV.1 'Stress' (p. 24, viewed) and p. 736, sec. V 'Diacritical Signs and Accents', rule A and 1st Note; article = pp. 229-296 of archive.org item (open)
3745.prule: Word stress on the final syllable (all Mugil District languages treated, Garus/Em included; only the Ate speech = Murupi excepted); a listed set of unaccented suffixes/postpositions does not take stress, so the root-final syllable keeps it; verbal suffixes take the stress; other exceptions marked with an acute in the wordlist
3745.srule: Only in reduplicated or compounded words: each component keeps a secondary stress on its own accented syllable, with the main stress on the ultimate (or penultimate) of the whole word per the general final-stress rule (serí, seríserí, seríserímo; bén sór > bénsórsór, afánfán, kanau ríkrík). For simple words no rhythmic secondary stress is given; the work only remarks that a long tense vowel (notably open ę) 'produces a secondary accent on a polysyllable, if it does not bear the stress itself' (p. 729; 'may produce the effect of a secondary accent', p. 735).
3745.quote: The basic tendency is to stress the last syllable; however, there are quite a few polysyllables which are not stressed on their last syllables.
